ocar.opportunity: Human Connectome Project–style MRI can map architecture and connectivity across many people, but invasive tracers that would ground those maps are not feasible in humans. Nonhuman primates let the same imaging methods be compared with quantitative tract tracing.
ocar.challenge: Functional connectivity from fMRI and tractographic connectivity from diffusion MRI need validation against long-distance connections measured with tracers. Laminar feedforward versus feedback features that define cortical hierarchy are invisible to noninvasive imaging.
ocar.action: Hayashi, Hou, Glasser, Autio, Knoblauch, Inoue-Murayama, Coalson, Yacoub, Smith, Kennedy, and Van Essen, in NeuroImage (2021), describe the NonHuman Primate Neuroimaging & Neuroanatomy Project (NHP_NNP): an international effort of six laboratories in five countries launched in 2018, adapting HCP-style protocols to macaque and marmoset.
ocar.resolution: The project aims to acquire high-resolution structural, functional, and diffusion MRI plus behavioral measures from over 100 macaques and marmosets; quantitative classical and next-generation tracer maps of cortical and subcortical projections; immunocytochemical cell-type maps for areal boundaries; and, in some macaques, ultra-high-resolution 10.5 T imaging at Minnesota. Advanced statistical modeling is intended to compare tracer-based and MRI-based connectivity and to relate genetics and sociality-associated behavior to individual variability.
ocar.future_work: This is a perspective on ongoing collection and analysis, not a finished atlas. Deliverables named in the extract include combined neuroimaging–neuroanatomy atlases, validation of noninvasive measures, and translation of improved methods to large human cohorts.

summaries.beginner: Human brain scans cannot be checked with dye tracers. This project scans macaque and marmoset monkeys with the same MRI methods used in people, then compares those maps with gold-standard anatomical tracing.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2021), Hayashi and colleagues present NHP_NNP, an HCP-style macaque and marmoset project across six labs in five countries (RIKEN, Kyoto University, Washington University, SBRI/IoN, Oxford, with Minnesota joining in 2020). Goals include HCP-style imaging in 100 macaques and marmosets, quantitative tract tracing mapped onto MRI volumes and surfaces, immunohistological cell-type maps of areas, comparison of imaging connectivity with tracer ground truth, genetics and social-behavior phenotyping, and 10.5 T imaging in some macaques. The piece is a project overview rather than a completed multi-subject connectome.
summaries.advanced: The extract is a perspective summarizing plans and current activities; it does not report finished tracer-versus-MRI correlation coefficients. “Over 100” animals is the imaging cohort target; anatomy is planned in a smaller macaque subset. Catalog organism is tagged other (primate). Head-coil and HCP-style preprocessing advances are cited from Autio et al. 2020 rather than newly quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Human brain scans cannot be checked with dye tracers. This project scans macaque and marmoset monkeys with the same MRI methods used in people, then compares those maps with gold-standard anatomical tracing.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can resolve nanometer ultrastructure, but large 3D datasets take hours to days to acquire, and speeding the microscope usually adds noise that blocks visualization and automated segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Advanced denoising exists, yet it is often locked in low-level code, needs fiddly parameter tuning, or is too slow for interactive use, so EM labs cannot easily try algorithms against their own data.
ocar.action: Roels, Vernaillen, Kremer, Gonçalves, Aelterman, Luong, Goossens, Philips, Lippens, and Saeys, in Nature Communications (2020), introduce DenoisEM, a GPU-accelerated ImageJ plugin whose computational backend uses the Quasar language for parallel restoration algorithms with interactive parameter tuning.
ocar.resolution: They report that DenoisEM is about one order of magnitude faster than related software and that acquisition can be sped by a factor of 4 without significantly affecting data quality. Denoising improved visualization and (semi-)automated segmentation of ultrastructure across volume-EM datasets; segmentation quality of denoised noisy inputs did not fall significantly relative to noise-free images for thresholding and pixel classification.
ocar.future_work: The discussion stresses that no single algorithm fits all 3D EM purposes because of a noise-reduction versus edge-blurring trade-off. Users still need to choose filters (bilateral, anisotropic diffusion, BLS-GSM, non-local means) for the downstream task.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope stacks get noisy if you scan them faster. This team ships an ImageJ plugin that denoises the pictures on a graphics card so labs can collect data more quickly without wrecking later tracing.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2020; 11:771), Roels and colleagues present DenoisEM, an interactive GPU-accelerated ImageJ denoising plugin. They report roughly 10× faster processing than related software and a 4× shorter acquisition without significantly affecting quality, with benefits for visualization and automated segmentation. Discussion notes that segmentation by thresholding or pixel classification did not drop significantly on denoised noisy inputs versus noise-free images, so throughput can rise without overexposure. The plugin is at http://bioimagingcore.be/DenoisEM.
summaries.advanced: “One order of magnitude faster” and “factor of 4” are the authors’ summary claims; per-algorithm wall-clock plots are shown for Matlab versus ImageJ versus Quasar but numeric table values are not excerpted here. The no-one-fits-all caveat and blur-versus-noise trade-off are stated qualitatively. Catalog method is volume EM.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope stacks get noisy if you scan them faster. This team ships an ImageJ plugin that denoises the pictures on a graphics card so labs can collect data more quickly without wrecking later tracing.

ocar.opportunity: To record from or manipulate a circuit you need genetic access to neurons connected to a starting population. Drosophila already has strong cell-type drivers, but until recently lacked a fully genetic retrograde transsynaptic tracer.
ocar.challenge: Anterograde tools (trans-Tango, TRACT) walk downstream from sensory neurons; motor and other output cells instead need a retrograde label of their inputs. Highly divergent connections are a hard test of false positives and misses.
ocar.action: Cachero, Gkantia, Bates, Frechter, Blackie, McCarthy, Sutcliffe, Strano, Aso, and Jefferis present BAcTrace (Botulinum-Activated Tracer), a genetically encoded retrograde system based on engineered Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin A that travels retrogradely to activate a silent transcription factor, validated in the Drosophila olfactory system.
ocar.resolution: They validated BAcTrace at three olfactory connections and showed that labeled partners can be recorded electrophysiologically. In a highly divergent circuit, BAcTrace correctly identified 12 of 16 connections previously observed by electron microscopy.
ocar.future_work: The catalog Nature Methods paper frames BAcTrace as a predominantly retrograde tool for fly connectomic analyses; remaining misses (4 of 16 in the EM comparison) and the need for matched driver lines are the practical limits for new circuits.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly geneticists can already light up chosen neurons, but not always the cells that talk to them. This paper engineers a Botox-based tracer that jumps backward across synapses and checks it against an electron-microscope wiring map.
summaries.intermediate: The catalog paper is Nature Methods (2020); the selected PDF is the matching bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2020.01.24.918656). Cachero and colleagues introduce BAcTrace, a genetically encoded retrograde transsynaptic label based on botulinum neurotoxin A. They validate it at three Drosophila olfactory connections, show electrophysiological access to labeled partners, and report that it recovered 12 of 16 EM-observed connections in a divergent circuit. Supplement tables list EM skeleton identifiers and partner/synapse counts for AV1 and PD2 neurons used in that comparison.
summaries.advanced: The PDF is the January 2020 preprint of the same BAcTrace paper, not a different study. “First fully genetically encoded retrograde transsynaptic labelling system” is the preprint wording. The 12/16 figure is the EM-grounded test; genotypes and skeleton IDs are in supplements rather than a single accuracy metric. Catalog stages list proofreading; the work is a genetic tracer, not EM proofreading.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly geneticists can already light up chosen neurons, but not always the cells that talk to them. This paper engineers a Botox-based tracer that jumps backward across synapses and checks it against an electron-microscope wiring map.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila offers a numerically simpler brain with sophisticated learning behavior, so olfactory associative memory can be dissected from genes to single identified neurons.
ocar.challenge: Human-scale brains (the review cites 86 billion neurons and an estimated ~100 trillion synapses) are not reverse-engineerable cell by cell, so tractable models must still capture molecular, cellular, and circuit mechanisms of short-term memory.
ocar.action: Boto, Stahl, and Tomchik, in Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), review how olfactory associative memories are encoded in Drosophila, emphasizing short-term memory, forward genetics, reverse-engineered learning circuits, and physiology at major plasticity loci.
ocar.resolution: They argue that genetic screens have revealed many necessary genes, some cell-autonomous; that behavioral phenotypes can in some cases be ascribed to single neurons; and that imaging and physiology have localized learning-related plasticity. Connectomics projects are treated as expanding the anatomical roadmap for those functional studies.
ocar.future_work: Outlook items are more complete genetics and synaptic signaling (including single-cell transcriptomics), whole-nervous-system connectivity (citing Eichler et al. 2017 and Zheng et al. 2018), parallel functional analysis with better imaging and perturbation tools, and new conceptual/computational frameworks, with conservation toward human principles stated as the long-term payoff.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies can learn to link odors with reward or punishment. This review explains how that short-term memory is built from genes, single cells, and circuits, and why new wiring diagrams will speed the next experiments.
summaries.intermediate: Boto, Stahl, and Tomchik (Journal of Neurogenetics, 2020; 34:36–46) review Drosophila olfactory associative learning with a focus on short-term memory. They cover forward genetic screens, reverse engineering of learning circuits down to single neurons, and functional imaging/physiology at major plasticity loci. Connectome efforts are described as filling the anatomical roadmap rather than as results of this paper. The conclusions call for richer genetics and signaling, more complete connectivity, circuit-level functional analysis, and new computational ideas.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review, not a new volume or behavior dataset. Human neuron/synapse counts in the introduction are background, not measurements here. Specific mushroom-body compartment physiology is not numerically excerpted. PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies can learn to link odors with reward or punishment. This review explains how that short-term memory is built from genes, single cells, and circuits, and why new wiring diagrams will speed the next experiments.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM and related high-throughput EM produce thousands of serial sections of subcellular structure, but low contrast still makes segmentation and 3D visualization slow.
ocar.challenge: Deep networks help, yet they usually need thousands of carefully curated labels. The extract cites a figure of about $10 per μm³ for manual EM annotation, so large volumes become expensive, and published evaluation metrics remain sparse.
ocar.action: Khadangi, Boudier, and Rajagopal introduce EM-net, a scalable deep convolutional network with trainable rectifiers (TLU) for EM segmentation, evaluated on two datasets including a long-running EM stack segmentation competition (since 2012).
ocar.resolution: They report that EM-net variants beat current deep-learning methods on small- and medium-sized ground-truth sets, that ensembles of top base classifiers win across a wide variety of metrics, and that EM-net is less prone to false-positive mitochondria calls, with voting ensembles further reducing false negatives.
ocar.future_work: The conclusions propose extending EM-net to 3D volume segmentation and other imaging modalities. Catalog metadata lists bioRxiv; the DOI is the later IEEE ICPR 2021 publication of the same work.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of cells are low-contrast and expensive to outline by hand. This paper trains a neural net that needs fewer labels and combines several versions of the model to pick out mitochondria more cleanly.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2020; 10.1101/2020.02.03.933127; catalog DOI is IEEE ICPR 2021), Khadangi, Boudier, and Rajagopal present EM-net, a DCNN using trainable linear units. Evaluation uses two datasets, one from the 2012-era EM stack competition. They report better performance than contemporary deep methods on small- and medium-sized ground truth, with ensembles of top classifiers leading across metrics. Visualizations on cardiac test data color true positives, false positives, missing mitochondria, and true negatives; they argue EM-net variants are less false-positive-prone than VGG, batch-normalized U-Net, or CDeep3M.
summaries.advanced: Per-metric scores are not in the selected extract. The $10/μm³ annotation cost is cited from prior work, not measured here. “Competition since 2012” is not named as ISBI in this extract. Catalog journal is bioRxiv; the IEEE DOI is the conference version of the same paper. Method tag is FIB-SEM; one evaluation set is described as cardiac mitochondria.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of cells are low-contrast and expensive to outline by hand. This paper trains a neural net that needs fewer labels and combines several versions of the model to pick out mitochondria more cleanly.

ocar.opportunity: Brain-wide synapse counts would constrain connectivity models, but volume EM can only sample tiny fields while fluorescent MAGUK puncta can be imaged across whole sections.
ocar.challenge: Spinning-disk confocal densities are two-dimensional projections (puncta/100 μm²) and overestimate apparent synapse size relative to true PSDs; FIB-SEM gives true 3D densities (synapses/μm³) but cannot be applied brain-wide.
ocar.action: Santuy, Tomás-Roca, Rodríguez, González-Soriano, Zhu, Qiu, Grant, DeFelipe, and Merchán-Pérez, in Scientific Reports (2020), genetically label PSD95 and SAP102, count fluorescent puncta in mouse CA1 with spinning-disk confocal microscopy, count synapses in the same area with FIB-SEM, and derive a conversion ratio applied to previously published brain-wide SDM data.
ocar.resolution: They report the highest estimated synapse densities in isocortex, olfactory areas, hippocampal formation, and cortical subplate; low densities in pallidum, hypothalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum; and a wide range in striatum and thalamus. In CA1 they separately analyzed excitatory and inhibitory synapses and sizes in strata oriens, radiatum, and lacunosum-moleculare. SDM (84 nm/pixel) overestimated PSD95 puncta size versus FIB-SEM PSDs (5 nm/pixel).
ocar.future_work: The conversion yields a minimum density estimate because MAGUK labels excitatory synapses and SDM can miss small or perpendicular synapses and merge overlapping puncta. Brain-wide claims inherit those biases plus the assumption that the CA1 ratio travels to other regions.

summaries.beginner: Counting every synapse in a whole brain with an electron microscope is impractical. This team measures real 3D synapse density in a bit of mouse hippocampus, then uses that as a ruler to turn fluorescent synapse snapshots from many other regions into estimated densities.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2020; 10:14014), Santuy and colleagues combine PSD95/SAP102 genetic labeling and spinning-disk confocal microscopy with FIB-SEM in mouse CA1. They convert FIB-SEM 3D densities (synapses/μm³) versus SDM 2D puncta (puncta/100 μm²) into a factor applied to published SDM maps. Highest densities are reported in isocortex, olfactory areas, hippocampal formation, and cortical subplate; lowest in pallidum, hypothalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum; striatum and thalamus vary widely. Discussion explains why SDM overestimates puncta size (scatter/glare/blur, 84 versus 5 nm/pixel, optical-section overlap).
summaries.advanced: Numeric conversion-factor values and per-stratum synapse densities are not in the selected extract. Brain-wide numbers are estimates from applying a CA1-derived ratio to prior SDM data, described as minimum densities of MAGUK-labeled excitatory synapses, not total EM synapses everywhere. Catalog organism is untagged; the tissue is mouse.

plain_language_summary: Counting every synapse in a whole brain with an electron microscope is impractical. This team measures real 3D synapse density in a bit of mouse hippocampus, then uses that as a ruler to turn fluorescent synapse snapshots from many other regions into estimated densities.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans and Pristionchus pacificus last shared an ancestor about 100 million years ago and occupy different habitats with different behaviors, so comparing identified amphid neurons can show what actually changes in a compact nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Without C. elegans-style winged AWx endings, homology assignments in P. pacificus rest on a bundle of weaker characters, and some pairs (especially AWA and ASI) lack discriminating features.
ocar.action: Hong, Riebesell, Bumbarger, Cook, Carstensen, Sarpolaki, Cochella, Castrejón, Moreno, Sieriebriennikov, Hobert, and Sommer, in eLife (2019), assign amphid, first-layer interneuron, and internal-receptor homologies using soma position, axon projections, dye filling, and related traits, then reconstruct a synaptic wiring diagram of amphid sensory and interneurons in P. pacificus.
ocar.resolution: Neuron number and soma position are highly conserved, but several amphid cilia differ, notably the absence of winged cilia in P. pacificus. Connectivity shows both conservation and divergence relative to C. elegans, with little change in the relative neighborhood of processes. The impact statement argues that evolutionary novelty lies in sensory specializations and synaptic partner choice inside invariant, prepatterned processes rather than in cell number or targeting.
ocar.future_work: The authors want cell-specific functional tests (for example AM5/ASE salt, AM12/AFD thermotaxis, AM3/AWA and AM7/AWC olfaction) and, longer term, cell-lineage reconstruction to resolve remaining homology uncertainty. They note little overlap in olfactory profiles and that markers such as GPCRs evolve quickly.

summaries.beginner: Two nematode worms split about 100 million years ago. This paper matches their nose-sensor neurons one-for-one and finds that cell number and positions stayed put while the fine sensory endings and who synapses with whom changed.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2019; 8:e47155; catalog journal lists bioRxiv), Hong and colleagues compare P. pacificus and C. elegans amphid systems. Homologies use soma position, axons, sheath entry, cilium number, dye filling, and interneuron connections. Number and soma position are conserved; winged amphid cilia are absent in P. pacificus. An amphid wiring diagram shows conserved and divergent synapses but stable process neighborhoods. Discussion assigns high confidence to ASH, ADL, ASJ, and AFD homologs and lower confidence to AWA and ASI, with remaining identities by elimination; reporter conservation is mixed (Ppa-che-1 versus Ppa-odr-7).
summaries.advanced: This is not a whole-brain connectome; it is amphid sensory neurons plus first-layer interneurons. Homology confidence is explicitly uneven. Catalog datasets tag DS01 C. elegans (White+); the new reconstruction is P. pacificus. Last-common-ancestor timing (~100 million years) is cited from Nei et al. and Prabh et al., not re-derived here.

plain_language_summary: Two nematode worms split about 100 million years ago. This paper matches their nose-sensor neurons one-for-one and finds that cell number and positions stayed put while the fine sensory endings and who synapses with whom changed.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a complete anatomical wiring diagram of 118 hermaphrodite neuron classes among 302 neurons, so a matching gene-expression map could link molecular identity to anatomy and synapses.
ocar.challenge: Single-cell RNA-seq catalogs in more complex brains cannot yet be assigned to fully identified, wired cell types. Some rare worm classes still drop out of clusters when few cells are captured.
ocar.action: Taylor, Santpere, Reilly, Glenwinkel, Poff, McWhirter, Xu, Weinreb, Basavaraju, Cook, Barrett, Abrams, Vidal, Cros, Rafi, Šestan, Hammarlund, Hobert, and Miller, on bioRxiv (2019), report CeNGEN single-cell transcriptomes of the mature hermaphrodite nervous system, with public browsers at cengen.org and SCeNGEA.
ocar.resolution: They generated transcriptomes for 52,412 neurons resolving into clusters for 109 of 118 canonical classes. Molecular signatures further split classes into subtypes, often distinguished by neuropeptide-related genes (examples in the extract include nlp-56 in RMG, nlp-17 in PVQ, and differential nlp-43/flp-4/flp-8 among AQR, PQR, and URX). Genes detected per class ranged from 1116 to 14,970 (median 7472) across 11 to 6,706 cells per class (median 228).
ocar.future_work: The authors expect the catalog to support mechanisms of lineage, anatomy, connectivity, and function. Remaining missing classes and mixed clusters (for example ALM/PLM, pharyngeal I2/I3) are attributed to small cell counts; a fitted curve predicts about 200 more detected genes for a 10% increase in cells in the sampled range.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram names every neuron type, but not which genes each type uses. This preprint profiles tens of thousands of single neurons and matches most of those types, with extra splits often marked by different neuropeptides.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2019; 10.1101/737577), Taylor and colleagues of the CeNGEN consortium report scRNA-seq of the mature C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous system: 52,412 neurons as clusters for 109 of 118 anatomical classes. Subtypes are often distinguished by neuropeptide genes; reporter checks include nlp-56 in RMG and nlp-17 in PVQ. Data are at cengen.org and SCeNGEA. Detected genes per class scale with cell number (median 7472 genes from a median 228 cells).
summaries.advanced: This is a 2019 preprint; later journal versions may expand coverage beyond 109/118. The selected “discussion” region is figure legends and acknowledgements, not a formal limitations section. Nine classes remain unresolved. Catalog dimension is graph-analysis; the product is a transcriptome atlas aligned to the White-style connectome, not a new graph.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram names every neuron type, but not which genes each type uses. This preprint profiles tens of thousands of single neurons and matches most of those types, with extra splits often marked by different neuropeptides.

ocar.opportunity: Cell-type-specific synapse maps in intact tissue would let labs quantify inhibitory input patterns with confocal imaging instead of sparse paired recordings or EM.
ocar.challenge: Overexpressed synaptic tags can change synapse number or physiology, and saturated immunohistochemical labeling of mixed axons is hard to assign to one presynaptic class.
ocar.action: Kuljis, Park, Telmer, Lee, Ackerman, Bruchez, and Barth, in eNeuro (2019), express fluorogen-activating protein or YFP fused to a postsynaptic neuroligin-1 targeting sequence (FAP/YFPpost), together with cytoplasmic dTomato, in mouse somatosensory cortex, and align puncta with Cre-dependent YFP in PV, SST, or VIP axons.
ocar.resolution: FAPpost did not alter mEPSC or mIPSC properties. Automated detection showed PV as the predominant inhibitory source onto L2/3 pyramids at soma and dendrites, especially the primary apical dendrite; SST inputs interleaved with PV on secondary- and higher-order branches; VIP inputs onto L2/3 pyramids were rare.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion asks for volumetric imaging in cleared or expanded tissue of the full dendritic tree, more molecular markers of synapse type, better presynaptic constructs, and infrastructure for large anatomic datasets.

summaries.beginner: It is hard to count which inhibitory cells synapse onto a cortical pyramid. This paper paints the pyramid’s synapses one color and the inhibitory axons another, then shows parvalbumin cells dominate while VIP contacts are scarce.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2019; 6:ENEURO.0193-19.2019), Kuljis and colleagues introduce FAP/YFPpost, a neuroligin-1–targeted fluorescent postsynaptic label. Sparse AAV expression with dTomato in mouse somatosensory cortex, combined with saturated PV, SST, or VIP axon labeling, allowed automated puncta–neurite apposition onto L2/3 pyramids. PV inputs predominated at soma and dendrites and were concentrated on the primary apical dendrite; SST mixed with PV on higher-order branches; VIP contacts were rare. FAPpost left miniature EPSCs and IPSCs unchanged.
summaries.advanced: Synapses are putative fluorescence appositions, not EM-confirmed. VIP “rare” is qualitative in the significance statement. Catalog stage is alignment; the paper is fluorescence connectomics of inhibitory subtypes onto L2/3 pyramids in barrel cortex. Overexpression artifacts are discussed as a motivation for the reagents, not as a residual quantified bias.

plain_language_summary: It is hard to count which inhibitory cells synapse onto a cortical pyramid. This paper paints the pyramid’s synapses one color and the inhibitory axons another, then shows parvalbumin cells dominate while VIP contacts are scarce.

ocar.opportunity: A high-fidelity micro-scale map of mammalian neurons and their physical contacts would support structure–function models and documentation of neuropathology.
ocar.challenge: Dense 3D image stacks still force largely manual neuron identification, which is slow and biased, and existing automatic or semi-automatic segmentation tools have uneven accuracy and validation metrics.
ocar.action: Magliaro, Callara, Vanello, and Ahluwalia, in Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology (2019), mini-review algorithms and software for single-neuron segmentation, validation metrics, tissue-clearing advances (including CLARITY), and emerging subcellular imaging.
ocar.resolution: They argue that clearing improves optical access and stack quality and could enable more efficient segmentation, but methods applied to clarified tissue have not yet yielded volumetric or topological single-neuron information. They highlight a shift from node-only tracing metrics toward whole-neuron volumetric and topological comparison.
ocar.future_work: Membrane probes (for example MemBright), STORM, whole-cell super-resolution (~50 nm in cited examples), and SOFI will require new algorithms for spines and thin neurites. They call for integrated, open-science pipelines for a structural connectome.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every neuron in a mammal brain by hand is too slow. This short review surveys computer tools for carving single cells out of 3D images, plus clearing and super-resolution methods that will make those tools even more necessary.
summaries.intermediate: Magliaro and colleagues (Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology, 2019) review automatic and semi-automatic single-neuron segmentation, validation metrics, and tissue clarification. They position robust dense-cell segmentation as the bottleneck to a mammalian structural connectome and note that published clarified-tissue methods still lack volumetric/topological single-neuron output. Future directions include membrane probes and super-resolution (tens of nanometers) that will demand algorithms for spines and thin neurites.
summaries.advanced: This is a mini-review, not a new segmenter or dataset. Super-resolution figures (order-of-magnitude improvement; 50 nm examples) are cited from other papers. Catalog stage is segmentation.

plain_language_summary: Tracing every neuron in a mammal brain by hand is too slow. This short review surveys computer tools for carving single cells out of 3D images, plus clearing and super-resolution methods that will make those tools even more necessary.

ocar.opportunity: Resting-state fMRI connectivity can define a robust endophenotype in Fmr1-/y mice, a Fragile X model, and would be more useful if it could also detect circuit-level effects of drugs.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether this macroscopic connectivity measure is sensitive enough to pick up pharmacological rescue, and whether any rescue would track behavior and white-matter structure.
ocar.action: Zerbi, Markicevic, Gasparini, Schroeter, Rudin, and Wenderoth, in NeuroImage (2019), inhibited mGluR5 with AFQ056/Mavoglurant and used rs-fMRI plus diffusion-weighted imaging in Fmr1-/y mice, focusing on circuits related to social behavior.
ocar.resolution: Fmr1-/y mice showed impaired social interaction, reduced connectivity in three main functional networks, and altered network topology. At group level, Mavoglurant rescued neither abnormal social behavior nor white-matter abnormalities, but it had a genotype-specific effect of restoring functional connectivity in some, not all, of those circuits.
ocar.future_work: The abstract concludes that rs-fMRI connectivity can detect system-level mGluR5 inhibition, but effects are circuit-confined, so behavioral benefits may be restricted to narrow functional domains.

summaries.beginner: A mouse model of Fragile X has odd brain-network coupling on MRI. This study asks whether an mGluR5 drug puts those networks back, and finds that some circuits improve on the scan even when social behavior and white matter do not.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2019), Zerbi and colleagues test whether Mavoglurant (AFQ056), an mGluR5 inhibitor, restores connectivity in Fmr1-/y mice. Using rs-fMRI and DWI, they replicate impaired social interaction, reduced connectivity in three main functional networks, and altered topology. Group-level Mavoglurant did not rescue social behavior or white-matter abnormalities, but restored functional connectivity in a genotype-specific way in some affected circuits. The abstract treats rs-fMRI as sensitive to pharmacological change yet spatially limited.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the file is van der Lei and Kooy, Biomedicines 2025, “From Discovery to Innovative Translational Approaches in 80 Years of Fragile X Syndrome Research,” not Zerbi et al. 2019 on Mavoglurant in Fmr1 knockout mice. This card uses only the catalog abstract. Do not treat CGG-repeat genetics, CRISPR/ASO programs, or 1-in-4000 incidence figures from the PDF as results of this paper. Catalog organism is untagged; the abstract is mouse FXS.

plain_language_summary: A mouse model of Fragile X has odd brain-network coupling on MRI. This study asks whether an mGluR5 drug puts those networks back, and finds that some circuits improve on the scan even when social behavior and white matter do not.

ocar.opportunity: Left–right brain asymmetry is a core human trait that may shift in psychiatric disease, but small studies have left both the healthy map and the clinical effects uncertain.
ocar.challenge: Findings were inconsistent, often underpowered, and it was unclear which structures are asymmetrical on average and how age, sex, and other biological variables relate to that variability.
ocar.action: Kong, Postema, Guadalupe, de Kovel, Boedhoe, Hoogman, Mathias, van Rooij, Schijven, Glahn, Medland, Jahanshad, Thomopoulos, Turner, Buitelaar, van Erp, Franke, Fisher, van den Heuvel, Schmaal, Thompson, and Francks, in Human Brain Mapping, review six ENIGMA-Laterality Working Group studies of gray-matter morphological asymmetry.
ocar.resolution: Total sample sizes were roughly 3,500 to 17,000, one to two orders of magnitude larger than typical earlier work. They report a population-level average-asymmetry map including a fronto-occipital gradient of cortical thickness asymmetry, with reproducibility illustrated across datasets. Autism spectrum disorder was associated with subtly reduced cortical-thickness asymmetry at widely distributed regions; pediatric obsessive–compulsive disorder with altered subcortical asymmetry; major depressive disorder was not significantly associated with asymmetry changes.
ocar.future_work: Ongoing ENIGMA work is examining other disorders, and the authors describe a groundwork for possibly identifying shared genetic contributions to asymmetry and disease.

summaries.beginner: People’s left and right brain halves differ a little, and psychiatry has long wondered if those differences change in illness. This consortium paper pools thousands of MRI scans to map typical asymmetry and test a few diagnoses at a much larger scale.
summaries.intermediate: Kong and colleagues (Human Brain Mapping; received 2019, published 2022, 43:167–181) summarize six ENIGMA-Laterality gray-matter asymmetry studies with samples of about 3,500–17,000. They describe a population map of average asymmetry, including a fronto-occipital cortical-thickness gradient, and effects of age, sex, handedness, and brain volume. ASD associated with subtly reduced cortical-thickness asymmetry at many regions; pediatric OCD with altered subcortical asymmetry; MDD not significantly associated. Effect sizes were estimated in large international samples rather than single-site case–control studies.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text is mostly front matter plus the reference list, so quantitative effect sizes are those stated in the abstract. Catalog year is 2019 (submission); the Wiley pagination is 2022. This is a consortium review of morphological asymmetry, not a synaptic connectome. Catalog axis is health_translation.

plain_language_summary: People’s left and right brain halves differ a little, and psychiatry has long wondered if those differences change in illness. This consortium paper pools thousands of MRI scans to map typical asymmetry and test a few diagnoses at a much larger scale.

ocar.opportunity: Animal brains destined for spatial omics, circuit tracing, or connectomic EM are routinely perfusion-fixed through the vasculature; translating those methods to humans means using autopsy tissue.
ocar.challenge: Brain banks typically immerse brains in fixative, which limits preservation. Whether perfusion is practical in banks, and how much it improves histology, had not been systematically reviewed.
ocar.action: McFadden, Walsh, Richter, Soudant, Bryce, Hof, Fowkes, Crary, and McKenzie, in Acta Neuropathologica Communications (2019), systematically reviewed human-brain perfusion fixation (protocol preregistered at OSF).
ocar.resolution: They screened 4,489 abstracts and 214 full texts and included 35 studies reporting perfusion of 558 human brains. Methods varied (in situ versus ex situ, vessels, washouts, fixatives, pressures, postfixation). A qualitative synthesis found moderate-confidence evidence that perfusion yields equal or greater subjective histology quality than immersion for relatively large tissue volumes, in equal or less time. Since the mid-1970s ex situ perfusion became more common; more recent work sometimes perfuses one hemisphere to leave the other freezable.
ocar.future_work: They recommend comparing in situ versus ex situ routes, testing washout solutions, and defining which donors actually benefit versus immersion. Downsides include edema or uneven fixation with cerebrovascular disease, plus logistical cost. Better perfusion would enable high-resolution ex vivo imaging, spatial profiling, tracing, and connectomics.

summaries.beginner: Animal brains are usually fixed by pumping chemical through blood vessels; human banked brains are usually soaked. This review gathers decades of human perfusion attempts and concludes the pictures often look as good or better, and not slower.
summaries.intermediate: McFadden et al. (Acta Neuropathologica Communications, 2019; 7:146) systematically reviewed perfusion fixation in human brain banking. From 4,489 abstracts and 214 full texts they included 35 studies (558 brains). Approaches vary widely. Moderate-confidence qualitative evidence indicated equal or better subjective histology than immersion for large volumes, in equal or less time. Conclusions note a historical shift from in situ to ex situ perfusion and later single-hemisphere protocols, alongside risks of edema/uneven fixation and substantial practical barriers versus simple immersion.
summaries.advanced: Evidence grade is moderate-confidence qualitative synthesis, not a meta-analytic effect size on connectomic EM quality. No single recommended recipe emerges. Catalog stages include proofreading; this paper is about specimen preparation for banking, not synapse proofreading.

plain_language_summary: Animal brains are usually fixed by pumping chemical through blood vessels; human banked brains are usually soaked. This review gathers decades of human perfusion attempts and concludes the pictures often look as good or better, and not slower.

ocar.opportunity: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) send axons to many brain targets that control circadian and pupillary function; a whole-neuron CLEM label could show whether those terminals look the same everywhere.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy cannot resolve bouton class or dendro-dendritic synapses, and conventional EM tracers do not easily follow the same genetically defined axons across distant nuclei.
ocar.action: Kim, Rios, Le, Perez, Phan, Bushong, Deerinck, Liu, Ellisman, Lev-Ram, Ju, Panda, Yoon, Hirayama, Mure, Hatori, Ellisman, and Panda, in Cell Reports (2019), use a membrane-targeted genetic CLEM probe in melanopsin RGCs and examine terminals in SCN, OPN, and lateral geniculate subregions.
ocar.resolution: Despite ipRGCs being the only direct retinal input to OPN and SCN, arbors and boutons differed markedly by target. SCN contained a dendro-dendritic chemical synapse (DDCS) network, with ipRGC axons preferentially contacting DDCS-linked cells. About 10% of SCN dendrites formed DDCSs at ~2 per 100 μm; ipRGC boutons were less than 15% of incoming synapses on SCN dendrites overall but up to 40% (distal) or 30% (proximal) on pre-DDCS dendrites. Distal dendrites almost all received ipRGC input, whereas nearly half of ventral SCN neurons lacked ipRGC input on somata or proximal dendrites.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the methods as a template for other long-distance CLEM circuits. Functional interpretations (coincidence detection over a large visual field; weighting against IGL, raphe, PVT, and local input) are hypotheses from the architecture, not new physiology.

summaries.beginner: A special class of retinal cells tells the brain about overall light for clocks and pupils. This study tags those cells for both light and electron microscopy and finds that their endings look different in each brain target, including an unusual dendrite-to-dendrite network in the clock nucleus.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell Reports (2019; 29:628–644.e6), Kim and colleagues express a membrane-targeted CLEM tag in melanopsin ipRGCs and reconstruct terminals in SCN, OPN, and LGN subregions. Terminal architecture differs by target. In SCN they describe DDCSs (~10% of dendrites; ~2 DDCSs per 100 μm) that are enriched for ipRGC input (up to 40%/30% of synapses on pre-DDCS distal/proximal dendrites), while ipRGCs are <15% of all incoming synapses on SCN dendrites. Discussion links class 2 boutons in SCN versus class 1 in OPN to photoentrainment versus other functions.
summaries.advanced: Percentages and DDCS rates are those stated in the discussion extract. “Only direct retinal input to OPN and SCN” is the authors’ framing. Catalog dataset DS09/DS10 is mouse retina; much of the EM is in retinorecipient brain, not retina itself. PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: A special class of retinal cells tells the brain about overall light for clocks and pupils. This study tags those cells for both light and electron microscopy and finds that their endings look different in each brain target, including an unusual dendrite-to-dendrite network in the clock nucleus.

ocar.opportunity: A cortical area receives and sends projections to dozens of others, so the brain needs a way to “gate in” one pathway and “gate out” another—for example vision versus audition in a noisy café.
ocar.challenge: Large-scale directed weighted connectomes (macaque, mouse) and models of global dynamics make pathway gating urgent, but the circuit mechanism is not settled, and inhibitory-cell classification is still being refined.
ocar.action: Wang and Yang, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2018), review experimental and computational evidence that a disinhibitory motif of three non-overlapping interneuron classes implements flexible pathway gating, and that the motif becomes more prominent from sensory to association cortex.
ocar.resolution: They summarize a canonical motif predicted by modeling: PV cells control pyramidal spike output at the soma, SST cells control dendritic input, and VIP-type cells disinhibit by targeting SST. They compare this input-gating picture with alternative or complementary gating mechanisms and note area-to-area quantitative differences that could yield different dynamical regimes.
ocar.future_work: Testable predictions include control signals acting through VIP and SST rather than pyramids. A direct test would require cell-type-specific physiology and manipulation during tasks that demand flexible routing. Transcriptomics may define subclasses and areal gradients; psychiatric gating deficits are flagged as related.

summaries.beginner: Your cortex has too many incoming cables to listen to all of them at once. This review argues that a three-part inhibitory circuit can open one pathway and close another, and that this motif is stronger in association areas than in early sensory areas.
summaries.intermediate: Wang and Yang (Current Opinion in Neurobiology, 2018; 49:75–83) review “pathway gating” via a disinhibitory motif. They place the problem against new macaque and mouse inter-areal matrices and argue that PV, SST, and VIP-class interneurons form a canonical motif in which SST gates pyramidal inputs and VIP disinhibits. They highlight an increasing preponderance of the motif toward association cortex and contrast it with other gating ideas. Concluding remarks call for cell-type-specific tests during flexible routing tasks.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/theory piece, not a new connectome. The three-class motif is presented as a consensus supporting a prior model prediction. Area-gradient claims cite Kim et al. and related work rather than new counts here. PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Your cortex has too many incoming cables to listen to all of them at once. This review argues that a three-part inhibitory circuit can open one pathway and close another, and that this motif is stronger in association areas than in early sensory areas.

ocar.opportunity: Retinal prostheses electrically stimulate remaining inner retina to restore partial vision in diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and AMD, but control of ganglion-cell timing is limited once the circuit remodels.
ocar.challenge: Early cellular death, anatomical change, and spontaneous firing in degenerating retina likely interfere with stimulation. Clinical devices still yield coarse perception; the extract cites Argus II letter recognition with best measured acuity 20/1260 and only 55% of electrodes effective in trials—as background, not this paper’s measurement.
ocar.action: Loizos, Marc, Humayun, Anderson, Jones, and Lazzi, in IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering (2018), combine a connectome-based retinal network (morphology and synapses) with an admittance-method model of tissue and electrodes, then computationally “degenerate” the retina and compare stimulation waveforms, including a proposed asymmetric biphasic pulse.
ocar.resolution: Stimulation thresholds of ON ganglion cells did not notably change after beginning-stage degeneration. Simulated asymmetric biphasic waveforms subdued spontaneous firing using comparable energy to symmetric pulses and increased control over ganglion-cell firing patterns.
ocar.future_work: The authors hope the waveform can raise efficacy of implanted devices but state that scaling to clinic still needs experimental validation. The framework is offered for further efficiency recommendations as degeneration progresses.

summaries.beginner: When the retina degenerates, leftover cells fire noisily and prosthetic electrodes struggle to talk to them. This modeling paper tests shock waveforms and proposes an uneven two-phase pulse that quiets that noise so timing is easier to control.
summaries.intermediate: Loizos et al. (IEEE TNSRE, 2018; 26:1111–1120) present a multiscale model pairing a connectome-based inner-retina network with bulk-tissue/prosthesis electronics. They analyze ON ganglion-cell threshold and range in healthy versus early-degenerated retina for existing waveforms and propose asymmetric biphasic current pulses. Thresholds did not notably vary after beginning degeneration; simulations indicated better control of firing by suppressing spontaneous activity at similar energy to symmetric biphasic pulses.
summaries.advanced: Argus II acuity and electrode-success figures are cited from clinical literature in the introduction, not produced by this model. Results are computational. Catalog dataset DS09/DS10 is mouse retina; the paper is a degenerated-retina stimulation model using connectome-informed morphology. Asymmetric pulses were considered in prior experiments the authors cite.

plain_language_summary: When the retina degenerates, leftover cells fire noisily and prosthetic electrodes struggle to talk to them. This modeling paper tests shock waveforms and proposes an uneven two-phase pulse that quiets that noise so timing is easier to control.

ocar.opportunity: A male C. elegans connectome now sits beside the hermaphrodite map, so sexual dimorphism and the circuits for egg-laying, copulation, and mate search can be described at identified-neuron resolution.
ocar.challenge: Sex-specific behaviors are not implemented only by sex-unique neurons; shared neurons also differ in synapses and help make navigational choices that affect reproductive success.
ocar.action: Emmons, in Annual Review of Neuroscience (2018), reviews neural circuits of sexual behavior using both connectomes.
ocar.resolution: The nervous system has 294 neurons shared by both sexes, plus 8 hermaphrodite-specific and 91 male-specific neurons. Sex-specific neurons are integrated into the shared network; in the male, 16% of input to the shared component comes from male-specific neurons. Those neurons mainly, but not only, control egg-laying versus copulation, acting with shared neurons. Considerable dimorphism exists inside the shared component, including synaptic connectivity. The extract’s mid-paper fragment treats egg-laying as a robust, highly regulated circuit in which eight motor neurons are primarily regulatory rather than essential for the laying event itself.
ocar.future_work: The review frames comprehensive description of dimorphism and circuit identification as newly possible; extrasynaptic signaling and environmental regulation (food, CO2, eggs in utero) are part of how even “simple” sexual circuits work.

summaries.beginner: Male and hermaphrodite roundworms share most of their neurons but not all of their wiring. This review uses both complete maps to explain how shared and sex-only cells together run mating and egg-laying.
summaries.intermediate: Emmons (Annual Review of Neuroscience, 2018; 41:349–369) reviews C. elegans sexual circuits in light of the adult male connectome plus the hermaphrodite map. Counts are 294 shared neurons, 8 hermaphrodite-specific, and 91 male-specific, with male-specific cells providing 16% of input onto the shared component. Dimorphism includes synapses among shared neurons. A section on egg-laying emphasizes regulation (bursts of ~10 eggs over 1–2 min, ~20 min quiescence; cited from Waggoner et al. 1998) and robustness to component defects.
summaries.advanced: This is a review. Neuron counts and the 16% figure are from the abstract. The selected PDF text jumps from the abstract into an egg-laying methods/history fragment rather than a dedicated conclusions section. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans (White+).

plain_language_summary: Male and hermaphrodite roundworms share most of their neurons but not all of their wiring. This review uses both complete maps to explain how shared and sex-only cells together run mating and egg-laying.

ocar.opportunity: Visual motion on the retina is parsed by parallel ganglion-cell circuits; the direction-selective circuit is the best-studied case in which function, connectomics, and models can be combined.
ocar.challenge: Motion encoding in the broader RGC population, and performance across natural image statistics, remain less mechanistically resolved than classic direction selectivity.
ocar.action: Wei, in Annual Review of Vision Science (2018), reviews neural mechanisms of motion processing in mammalian retina, focusing on direction selectivity (including starburst amacrine cells) and then other motion features.
ocar.resolution: The review emphasizes that multiple mechanisms are engaged dynamically and in a stimulus-dependent way to keep motion detection robust across conditions. Direction selectivity is presented as having been dissected in unprecedented detail with functional, connectomic, and modeling methods.
ocar.future_work: Open questions include mechanisms in broader RGC populations, tools to target specific cell types and motifs, and stimulus designs informed by natural-scene statistics that can reveal receptive-field properties missed by artificial stimuli.

summaries.beginner: When something moves on the eye, many types of retinal cells fire in parallel. This review explains how the famous direction-selective circuit works, and why other motion detectors in the retina still need better tools and more natural movies.
summaries.intermediate: Wei (Annual Review of Vision Science, 2018; 4:165–192) reviews motion processing in mammalian retina, with the main focus on the direction-selective circuit studied with physiology, connectomics, and models. Broader RGC motion features are discussed more briefly. The closing section argues that natural image statistics can recruit mechanisms invisible to standard artificial stimuli and that cell-type tools are needed for non-DS motion circuits.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new EM volume. Catalog dataset DS09/DS10 is mouse retina; the review is mammalian retina with mouse as a major source of DS-circuit detail. No new synapse counts appear in the selected extract.

plain_language_summary: When something moves on the eye, many types of retinal cells fire in parallel. This review explains how the famous direction-selective circuit works, and why other motion detectors in the retina still need better tools and more natural movies.

ocar.opportunity: In sensory cortex, intermingled neurons encode different stimulus attributes and send them to different long-range targets; knowing whether those output channels also keep separate local synapses would explain how parallel streams stay independent.
ocar.challenge: Like-to-like connectivity based on sensory responses is established, but the relationship between within-area synapses and long-range projection target was unclear.
ocar.action: Kim, Znamenskiy, Iacaruso, and Mrsic-Flogel, in Neuron (2018), examined local connectivity and visual responses of mouse primary visual cortex neurons that project to anterolateral (AL) versus posteromedial (PM) higher visual areas.
ocar.resolution: Layer 2/3 neurons projecting to different targets often had similar visual responses but avoided connecting with each other. Projection target, in addition to response similarity, therefore constrains local synaptic connectivity of AL and PM projection neurons. The authors propose that reduced crosstalk permits independent function of these output channels.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the independence of output channels as an interpretation of the avoided connections; further tests of function across areas are not specified in the catalog abstract.

summaries.beginner: Cells in visual cortex that send axons to different next-stage areas often see the world similarly. This paper finds they still avoid linking to each other locally, which may keep those output pipelines from mixing.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2018), Kim, Znamenskiy, Iacaruso, and Mrsic-Flogel map local connectivity and visual responses of mouse V1 neurons projecting to AL versus PM. Despite often-similar responses, L2/3 AL- and PM-projecting cells avoided synapses with each other. The authors conclude that projection target constrains local connectivity beyond response similarity and propose that this reduced crosstalk supports independent output channels.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the file is Butrus, Monday, Yoo, Feldman, and Shekhar, PLOS Biology 2025, “Molecular states underlying neuronal cell type development and plasticity in the postnatal whisker cortex,” not Kim et al. 2018 on segregated AL/PM projection neurons in V1. This card uses only the catalog abstract. Do not treat snRNA-seq of ~80,000 wS1 nuclei, ~250 temporally regulated genes, or whisker-deprivation results from the PDF as findings of this paper. Catalog organism is untagged; the abstract is mouse V1.

plain_language_summary: Cells in visual cortex that send axons to different next-stage areas often see the world similarly. This paper finds they still avoid linking to each other locally, which may keep those output pipelines from mixing.

ocar.opportunity: Night vision is encoded by rod bipolar cells and distributed into ON and OFF cone pathways through AII amacrine cells; a complete local map plus paired physiology can show what the intermediary actually passes on.
ocar.challenge: AIIs contact multiple OFF cone bipolar types, so preference, directionality, and which temporal components (transient versus sustained) survive to each target are not obvious from anatomy alone.
ocar.action: Graydon, Lieberman, Rho, Briggman, Singer, and Diamond, in Current Biology (2018), combine SBEM reconstructions with paired whole-cell recordings in mouse retina.
ocar.resolution: AIIs preferentially connect to OFF CBC2. Each reconstructed CBC2 made ribbons onto 3.0±0.9 AIIs and received input from 3.0±0.9 AIIs (n=6). AII→CBC2 signals were much larger than CBC2→AII. Transient RBC signals reached CBC2 with high fidelity; whether sustained components also arrived depended on network activation. CBC5 received both transient and sustained components. AIIs made about eight times as many synapses onto OFF CBCs as onto ganglion cells, with CBC2 receiving more AII input than all other targets combined.
ocar.future_work: Upper-bound divergence/convergence counts (a rod potentially influencing 12–40 CBC2s; a CBC2 collecting 432–1680 rods before shared-rod correction) ignore gap junctions and shared rods. GluMI/CBC1B could not be identified because the EM volume lacked INL somata.

summaries.beginner: In dim light, a specialized interneuron hands rod signals to both ON and OFF cone pathways. This paper maps those contacts in mouse retina and shows the cell does not copy the same message to every partner.
summaries.intermediate: Graydon et al. (Current Biology, 2018; 28:2739–2751.e3) reconstruct AII–OFF CBC connectivity with SBEM and test transfer with paired patch clamp. AIIs preferentially contact CBC2 (3.0±0.9 AIIs per CBC2 in both directions, n=6), with functionally asymmetric AII→CBC2 synapses. Transient RBC input reaches CBC2 reliably; sustained components depend on network state, whereas CBC5 gets both. Anatomy shows ~8× more AII synapses onto OFF CBCs than onto ganglion cells, and CBC2 as the dominant AII target.
summaries.advanced: The 12–40 and 432–1680 figures are bounding products of published divergence/convergence, not direct counts of unique rods. Gap junctions are not included. Catalog method is SBF-SEM (SBEM). PMC copy is an author manuscript. Selective transfer changing with background luminance is stated in the eTOC.

plain_language_summary: In dim light, a specialized interneuron hands rod signals to both ON and OFF cone pathways. This paper maps those contacts in mouse retina and shows the cell does not copy the same message to every partner.

ocar.opportunity: A refined mouse cortical parcellation plus quantitative retrograde tracing can test whether the mouse meso-connectome is a sparse directed graph or an almost-complete weighted graph like a denser version of macaque.
ocar.challenge: Earlier mouse matrices (notably Oh et al. 2014) reported much lower density. Tracer spill, fibers of passage, and parcellation error could inflate density if not controlled.
ocar.action: Gămănuţ, Kennedy, Toroczkai, Ercsey-Ravasz, Van Essen, Knoblauch, and Burkhalter, in Neuron (2018), made 27 retrograde tracer injections in 19 areas of a 47-area mouse neocortex parcellation, counted labeled neurons on flat mounts with multiple histological markers, and performed weighted graph analysis.
ocar.resolution: Connection weights to each area were lognormal over five orders of magnitude, yielding distinct connectivity profiles analogous to macaque. Graph density was 97%, versus 66% reported in macaque. Weighted analysis showed similar global efficiency to macaque but weaker spatial clustering. Consistency and profiles differed significantly from earlier mouse studies. Dominating-set analysis of the studied subgraph suggested the full matrix may indeed be 97% dense. Repeat injections with means above 24 labeled neurons were highly consistent.
ocar.future_work: The authors discuss remaining concerns about DY uptake by injured deep axons. They contrast their deterministic counts with probabilistic Allen connectivity (maximum 53% in Oh et al. 2014) and a rat meta-analysis (Bota et al. 2015).

summaries.beginner: Mouse cortical areas might be either sparsely or almost fully interconnected. This tracing study finds nearly every possible link exists, but the strengths of those links still give each area a unique fingerprint.
summaries.intermediate: Gămănuţ et al. (Neuron, 2018; 97:698–715.e10) report 27 retrograde injections into 19 of 47 mouse cortical areas. Weights are lognormal over five orders of magnitude with area-specific profiles. They report 97% connection density (versus 66% in macaque), similar global efficiency, and weaker spatial clustering than macaque. Findings differ from Oh et al. 2014. Technical checks include confined injection cores (27 of 102 injections fully analyzed) and high consistency when mean labeled neurons exceeded 24.
summaries.advanced: 97% is the reported cortical-graph density; dominating-set analysis is used to argue the unsampled full matrix may match. Density is much higher than Allen probabilistic maps; whether residual fiber-of-passage labeling remains is discussed, not fully excluded. Catalog organism is mouse. PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Mouse cortical areas might be either sparsely or almost fully interconnected. This tracing study finds nearly every possible link exists, but the strengths of those links still give each area a unique fingerprint.

ocar.opportunity: Large structural and physiological datasets make it possible, in principle, to simulate cortical activity under in-vivo-like visual conditions rather than only reduced in vitro circuits.
ocar.challenge: Quantitative models that are both anatomically detailed and match in vivo responses remain rare. Extreme simplifications may still capture some phenomena while breaking others.
ocar.action: Arkhipov, Gouwens, Billeh, Gratiy, Iyer, Wei, Xu, Abbasi-Asl, Berg, Buice, Cain, da Costa, de Vries, Denman, Durand, Feng, Jarsky, Lecoq, Lee, Li, Mihalas, Ocker, Olsen, Reid, Soler-Llavina, Sorensen, Wang, Waters, Scanziani, Koch, and colleagues, in PLOS Computational Biology (2018), publicly release a 45,000-neuron biophysical model of mouse V1 layer 4 with thalamic visual input, tested against published and new in vivo data including optogenetic perturbations.
ocar.resolution: Simulations reproduced many observations (grating-response magnitude, orientation selectivity, gamma, long-tailed rates, sparsity, variability trends, cortical amplification, LGN and Scnn1a perturbations). Rules of functional synaptic connectivity were critical to in silico versus in vivo agreement. After extreme simplification the model still did well on many measures, though quantitative agreement suffered. Training used a gray screen and a single 0.5 s grating, yet the model generalized across a larger stimulus battery.
ocar.future_work: The authors note omitted biology (active dendrites, few unique morphologies, no short-term plasticity, simplified LGN, missing interneuron types, other layers reduced to background). They suggest many L4 computations may be local, with other layers mainly modulatory. Code, model, and results are released to enable the next generation of data-driven in vivo models.

summaries.beginner: A huge computer model of one layer of mouse visual cortex is shown movies and compared with real recordings. Wiring rules between cells matter most; even a stripped-down version still gets many qualitative facts right.
summaries.intermediate: Arkhipov et al. (PLOS Computational Biology, 2018; 14:e1006535; catalog journal lists bioRxiv) present a 45,000-neuron layer-4 mouse V1 model with thalamic input. A stimulus battery plus optogenetic perturbations matched many in vivo features; functional connectivity rules were essential. A highly simplified model remained qualitatively usable but quantitatively worse. Despite training on gray plus one 0.5 s grating, responses generalized. Public resources are at the Allen Institute model portal; full simulation output is ~1 TB on request.
summaries.advanced: Catalog DOI/journal point to the published PLOS paper; the PDF matches that article. Agreement is described across observation types, not as a single score. Many biological simplifications are listed in the discussion. Catalog dataset tag DS12 is L4 barrel cortex, whereas this model is mouse V1 layer 4. Organism is mouse.

plain_language_summary: A huge computer model of one layer of mouse visual cortex is shown movies and compared with real recordings. Wiring rules between cells matter most; even a stripped-down version still gets many qualitative facts right.

ocar.opportunity: Misfolded tau (and synuclein) appear to spread on anatomical networks; a connectome-based network diffusion model (NDM) that already describes AD and FTD might also explain the stereotyped topography of progressive supranuclear palsy.
ocar.challenge: It was unknown whether NDM applies to PSP and whether direction of edges (anterograde soma-to-terminal versus retrograde versus undirected) matters for fitting atrophy/pathology maps.
ocar.action: Pandya, Mezias, and Raj, in Frontiers in Neurology (2017), apply directional and non-directional NDM to PSP, whose pathology is described as appearing first in striatum then in neighbors and connected cortex.
ocar.resolution: PSP was amenable to connectome-based NDM as previously used in AD and FTD. Fits to empirical data were significantly better with a directional human connectome than with a non-directional one; both anterograde and retrograde modes outperformed undirected transmission. They interpret this as structural-network mediation of spread, most likely trans-neuronal.
ocar.future_work: Limitations include a first-order linear model that assumes a static connectome, missing individual genetic/medication/onset variables, and the need for independent replication. Future work on striatal vulnerability and repeat length is flagged.

summaries.beginner: Some brain diseases seem to walk along the wires of the connectome. This study tests that idea in progressive supranuclear palsy and finds that keeping the direction of those wires in the model improves the match to real atrophy patterns.
summaries.intermediate: Pandya, Mezias, and Raj (Frontiers in Neurology, 2017; 8:692) apply a network diffusion model to PSP. They report that NDM, previously used for AD and FTD, also captures PSP topography, and that directional connectomes (anterograde and retrograde) fit empirical maps better than an undirected graph. Pathology is framed as beginning in striatum then involving neighbors and connected cortex. They conclude that intrinsic structural architecture mediates spread, likely trans-neuronally.
summaries.advanced: No numeric R² values appear in the selected extract. Directionality improves fit, but anterograde versus retrograde are both better than undirected rather than a single winning polarity. NDM assumes an unchanged network over time. Catalog has no organism tag; this is human neuroimaging/modeling. Typo “palspy” appears in the PDF keywords.

plain_language_summary: Some brain diseases seem to walk along the wires of the connectome. This study tests that idea in progressive supranuclear palsy and finds that keeping the direction of those wires in the model improves the match to real atrophy patterns.

ocar.opportunity: CA3 is classically treated as one autoassociative network for pattern completion, but spatial encoding and memory already differ along the proximodistal (transverse) axis.
ocar.challenge: Circuit mechanisms—intrinsic excitability and synaptic weights—that could explain those functional differences had not been mapped systematically across CA3a/b/c.
ocar.action: Sun, Sotayo, Cazzulino, Snyder, Denny, and Siegelbaum, in Neuron (2017), measure dorsal CA3 pyramidal intrinsic properties and synaptic connectivity and use a genetic memory-trace strategy during contextual fear memory retrieval.
ocar.resolution: Mossy-fiber synaptic strength decreases along the proximodistal axis while direct entorhinal excitation increases. Fear-memory reactivation is nonuniform and most robust in mid-CA3 (CA3b), the region with strongest net recurrent excitation (reduced recurrent I/E ratio). Gradients in resting potential, excitability, and sag were linear rather than abrupt, despite the traditional a/b/c labels. The mouse CA3 region contains over 100,000 neurons.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest that local-circuit heterogeneity contributes to distinct spatial encoding and behavioral roles of CA3 subregions. They note that CA2 versus CA3a boundaries remain a morphological/molecular issue.

summaries.beginner: The hippocampal area CA3 is often drawn as one uniform loop. This paper shows a smooth gradient: mossy-fiber input is stronger at one end, cortex input at the other, and memory-trace replay peaks in the middle.
summaries.intermediate: Sun et al. (Neuron, 2017; 95:656–672.e3) report proximodistal gradients in dorsal CA3: decreasing mossy-fiber strength, increasing entorhinal excitation, and peak contextual-fear reactivation in CA3b where net recurrent excitation is strongest. Traditional CA3a/b/c divisions are used for convenience; many electrophysiological parameters change linearly. A genetic tagging strategy (citing Denny/Cazzulino) showed weaker reactivation in CA3c than more distal CA3, with efficiency peaking in CA3b.
summaries.advanced: “Over 100,000 neurons” is a discussion statement about mouse CA3 size, not a new census. Reactivation is a genetic-trace readout, not EM connectivity. Catalog organism is mouse. PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: The hippocampal area CA3 is often drawn as one uniform loop. This paper shows a smooth gradient: mossy-fiber input is stronger at one end, cortex input at the other, and memory-trace replay peaks in the middle.

ocar.opportunity: If the energy needed to steer a network can be written in terms of which edges touch driver nodes, then connectomes can be compared and even edited for control performance.
ocar.challenge: Numerical control-energy calculations do not by themselves yield design rules. Clinical edge deletions (a single tract) need an analytic prediction of how control energy will change.
ocar.action: Kim, Soffer, Kahn, Vettel, Pasqualetti, and Bassett use linear network control theory to derive closed-form expressions linking driver-to-non-driver connections to minimum control energy, then apply them to high-resolution Drosophila, mouse, and human connectomes.
ocar.resolution: They report topological features that raise or lower control energy and, in the preprint extract, that connectomes of increasingly complex species are wired to reduce control energy. Cross-species comparison is used to argue that the human brain supports diverse dynamics at small energetic cost while remaining robust to perturbations. Single-edge removal is presented as a clinically accessible manipulation of control performance.
ocar.future_work: The extract includes a first-order approximation whose error versus unsimplified Gramians is checked numerically (Fig. 2b). Real brains are not linear time-invariant systems; the theory is a linear control approximation.

summaries.beginner: Steering a network takes energy that depends on how the “driver” nodes plug into the rest. Applied to fly, mouse, and human wiring diagrams, this theory suggests more complex brains are built to be cheaper to control and fairly robust if one connection is lost.
summaries.intermediate: The catalog paper is Nature Physics (2017; nphys4268); the selected PDF is the matching arXiv preprint “Topological Principles of Control in Dynamical Network Systems” (1702.00354). Kim and colleagues derive closed-form linear-control expressions relating driver–non-driver edges to minimum energy and apply them to Drosophila, mouse, and human connectomes. They argue more complex species reduce control energy and that the human brain supports diverse dynamics cheaply while remaining robust, including under single-edge deletions.
summaries.advanced: Preprint versus journal titles differ but authors and claims match; treat as the same paper. Catalog organism is tagged fly; the study is explicitly comparative across fly, mouse, and human. Linear LTI control is an approximation. Numeric energy values are not in the selected extract (later pages are derivations).

plain_language_summary: Steering a network takes energy that depends on how the “driver” nodes plug into the rest. Applied to fly, mouse, and human wiring diagrams, this theory suggests more complex brains are built to be cheaper to control and fairly robust if one connection is lost.

ocar.opportunity: A directed rat cortical connectome from tracing, paired with resting-state fMRI, can test how much empirical functional coupling is explained by anatomical weights and by simulations on that graph.
ocar.challenge: Structure–function correspondence can be inflated or distorted by parcellation mismatches, global-signal regression, motion, and anesthesia.
ocar.action: Díaz-Parra, Osborn, Canals, Moratal, and Sporns, in NeuroImage (2017), combine a curated meta-analysis tracing connectome with rs-fMRI from 14 anesthetized Wistar rats and run neural-mass simulations on the empirical anatomy.
ocar.resolution: Maximum Spearman correlation between BOLD functional-connection strength and anatomical weight was ρ = 0.48. Regions in the same functional community formed more mutual weighted anatomical connections, and functional communities were enriched in dense anatomical motifs not explained by lower-order topology. Simulated FC on the rat connectome reached a maximum Pearson correlation of ρ = 0.53 with measured FC.
ocar.future_work: Limitations discussed include incomplete rat connectome coverage, manual Swanson versus Paxinos matching, aggregating some ROIs, hemispheric averaging of 32 equal-volume ROIs, GSR plus scrubbing (minimum ~9 min windows), and urethane at 1.2 g/kg. They point to more complete tracing (e.g. Swanson et al. 2016) and better physiology as next steps.

summaries.beginner: In rats, the team compares a wiring diagram built from published tracer studies with resting-state MRI. Stronger anatomical links and certain dense motifs go with stronger functional coupling, and a simple simulation on the wiring partly recreates the MRI pattern.
summaries.intermediate: Díaz-Parra et al. (NeuroImage, 2017; 159:170–184) relate a directed rat cortical tracing connectome to rs-fMRI in 14 urethane-anesthetized Wistar rats. Peak Spearman structure–function correlation was ρ = 0.48; neural-mass simulations on the same anatomy reached Pearson ρ = 0.53 versus empirical FC. Same-community regions had more reciprocal weighted connections, and functional communities were enriched for dense anatomical motifs beyond lower-order topology.
summaries.advanced: ρ = 0.48 and 0.53 are maxima over the analyses reported, not a single universal coefficient. Anesthesia (urethane 1.2 g/kg) and GSR/motion pipelines are explicit caveats. Catalog dimension is proofreading; the work is structure–function modeling, not EM proofreading. Organism tag is other (rat).

plain_language_summary: In rats, the team compares a wiring diagram built from published tracer studies with resting-state MRI. Stronger anatomical links and certain dense motifs go with stronger functional coupling, and a simple simulation on the wiring partly recreates the MRI pattern.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomics is precise but slow and costly; converting synapses into DNA barcode pairs could use sequencing throughput instead of tracing axons across thousands of sections.
ocar.challenge: A 5 mm axon through 50 nm sections would, under the paper’s simple assumptions, need per-section tracing accuracy above 99.999% for even a 36% chance of a correct assignment—illustrating why automation remains hard.
ocar.action: Peikon, Kebschull, Vagin, Ravens, Sun, Brouzes, Corrêa, Bressan, and Zador, in Nucleic Acids Research (2017), present SYNseq: unique RNA barcodes targeted to synapses, protein–protein crosslinking of pre- and postsynaptic partners, extraction, and joining for sequencing.
ocar.resolution: Each biochemical piece (barcoding, protein joining, RNA joining) could be shown to work, including emulsion overlap RT-PCR joining in principle, but they could not recover many barcode pairs. In-droplet reverse transcription efficiency on the order of 1% implies both barcodes succeed in only about 0.01% of properly loaded droplets (0.01²), so joining—not barcoding or crosslinking—limited detection. In its current form SYNseq was unusable for biological circuit tracing.
ocar.future_work: They suggest optimizing droplets (perhaps with barcoded beads), or joining by RNA ligation, gap filling, or immobilization on beads/chips/gels, and co-expressing components via two RNA-binding domains. Catalog journal lists bioRxiv; the PDF is the NAR paper.

summaries.beginner: Instead of photographing every synapse, this method tries to read connections as paired DNA barcodes. The biochemistry mostly works, but stitching the two barcodes together is still far too inefficient to map a real circuit.
summaries.intermediate: Peikon et al. (Nucleic Acids Research, 2017; 45:e115; catalog journal lists bioRxiv) introduce SYNseq: synaptic RNA barcodes joined across engineered protein bridges for sequencing. Components function, but barcode joining failed at usable efficiency. They estimate ~1% in-droplet RT, hence ~0.01% of droplets with both barcodes reverse-transcribed, and therefore blame joining (especially RT) rather than barcoding or trans-synaptic complex formation. The published abstract states that failure to develop efficient joining precludes widespread application.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods paper that reports a negative practical result on joining. The 99.999% EM tracing illustration is a back-of-envelope motivation, not an empirical error rate. No circuit was mapped. Catalog stages include proofreading and graph analysis; those are aspirations, not delivered graphs.

plain_language_summary: Instead of photographing every synapse, this method tries to read connections as paired DNA barcodes. The biochemistry mostly works, but stitching the two barcodes together is still far too inefficient to map a real circuit.

ocar.opportunity: Without a formal link between network structure and emergent function it is hard to say how cortex processes stimuli in terms of synaptic architecture.
ocar.challenge: Standard undirected graph statistics ignore the direction of synaptic transmission and can miss higher-order organization such as cliques bound into cavities.
ocar.action: Reimann, Nolte, Scolamiero, Turner, Perin, Chindemi, Dłotko, Levi, Hess, and Markram, in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2017), build directed graphs that follow information flow and analyze a local neocortical network with algebraic topology.
ocar.resolution: They report an intricate previously unseen topology: an abundance of neuronal cliques bound into cavities that guide correlated activity. In response to stimuli, correlated activity binds synaptically connected neurons into functional cliques and cavities that evolve in a stereotypical sequence toward peak complexity. They propose that the brain processes stimuli by forming increasingly complex functional cliques and cavities.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the clique-and-cavity sequence as a proposed processing principle; further tests beyond the local neocortical network are not specified in the catalog abstract.

summaries.beginner: Looking at cortex as one-way streets instead of undirected wires reveals clumps of fully connected cells wrapped around holes. This paper argues those growing clumps and holes are how the network organizes activity after a stimulus.
summaries.intermediate: Reimann and colleagues (Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience, 2017) apply algebraic topology to directed synaptic graphs of a local neocortical network. Accounting for transmission direction, they describe abundant cliques of neurons bound into cavities that shape correlated activity. Stimuli elicit a stereotyped sequence of increasingly complex functional cliques and cavities. They propose this sequence as a missing structure–function link for how cortex processes stimuli.
