summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the file is Ercole, Marcolongo, Umari, and Baroni, “Gauge invariance of thermal transport coefficients,” a Journal of Low Temperature Physics / arXiv:1601.00158 molecular-dynamics paper, not Reimann et al. on neuronal cliques and cavities. This card uses only the catalog abstract. Do not treat Green–Kubo conductivity, Lennard-Jones fluids, or energy-flux gauge invariance from the PDF as results of this paper.

plain_language_summary: Looking at cortex as one-way streets instead of undirected wires reveals clumps of fully connected cells wrapped around holes. This paper argues those growing clumps and holes are how the network organizes activity after a stimulus.

ocar.opportunity: Many networks of scientific interest, including biological ones, have community structure—groups of vertices more likely to connect internally than to other groups—so practitioners need a critical guide to detection methods.
ocar.challenge: Community detection is ill-defined: there is no universal definition of community, nor agreed protocols for validation and algorithm comparison, which has produced confusion that slows the field.
ocar.action: Fortunato and Hric, in Physics Reports (2016; arXiv:1608.00163), write a user guide covering what communities are, validation (benchmarks, partition similarity, detectability, metadata), methods (spectral, overlapping, statistical inference, optimization, dynamics), software, and outlook.
ocar.resolution: They survey classic and modern views of communities, strengths and weaknesses of popular algorithms, and practical directions for use, emphasizing that identifying communities is not a single well-posed computational problem.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract is largely the introduction and table of contents; the outlook chapter itself is not in the excerpt. The paper’s stated aim is to reduce misconceptions and guide method choice rather than to introduce a new clustering algorithm.

summaries.beginner: Finding clusters in a network sounds simple until you notice nobody agrees what a cluster is. This long guide walks through the definitions, tests, and algorithms so you can pick a method without treating it as magic.
summaries.intermediate: Fortunato and Hric (Physics Reports, 2016; arXiv:1608.00163) provide a user guide to community detection. They frame clustering as ill-defined, review variables and classic versus modern views of communities, then organize validation (artificial benchmarks, similarity measures, detectability, structure versus metadata) and method families (how many clusters, consensus, spectral, overlapping, inference, optimization, dynamics, significance). Catalog journal lists arXiv.org; the DOI is the Physics Reports article.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text is the front of a long review (body extract ~8.5k characters) and does not include the outlook chapter or empirical brain-network results. No single recommended algorithm is in this excerpt (“Which method then?” is a TOC heading). Treat claims about software and best practice as the review’s program, not as numbers from this shard’s extract.

plain_language_summary: Finding clusters in a network sounds simple until you notice nobody agrees what a cluster is. This long guide walks through the definitions, tests, and algorithms so you can pick a method without treating it as magic.

ocar.opportunity: Comparing hermaphrodite and male C. elegans connectomes shows sexually dimorphic synapses among the 294 neurons present in both sexes, a chance to watch how shared neurons acquire sex-specific wiring.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear whether dimorphic connections are built from scratch in one sex or sculpted from an initially shared hybrid pattern, and whether sexual identity of pre- versus postsynaptic cells is instructive.
ocar.action: Oren-Suissa, Bayer, and Hobert, in Nature (2016), demonstrate sex-specific functions of shared neurons, follow synapse development across sexual maturation, and manipulate sexual identity and dimorphic transcription factors.
ocar.resolution: Many neurons first form synapses in both male and hermaphrodite patterns; sex-specific pruning then keeps a subset. Reversing sexual identity of either the pre- or the postsynaptic neuron alone switches connectivity to the opposite-sex pattern. A dimorphically expressed conserved transcription factor (DMD-5/11 acting with TRA-1 in the extract’s summary schematic) is necessary and sufficient for sex-specific connectivity. Timing of pruning requires additional timer mechanisms because dmd-5/11 are already dimorphic in embryos and L1.
ocar.future_work: The authors hypothesize that other neurons (for example AVA) have their own sex-specific dmd genes controlling pruning, and that heterochronic factors may time the onset of pruning.

summaries.beginner: Male and hermaphrodite worms share most neurons but not all of their synapses. This paper shows many connections are wired both ways at first, then each sex prunes the extras, under the control of the cell’s sexual identity and a conserved transcription factor.
summaries.intermediate: Oren-Suissa, Bayer, and Hobert (Nature, 2016; 533:206–211) start from dimorphic synapses among sex-shared C. elegans neurons (294 shared; 8 hermaphrodite-specific; 91 male-specific). Shared neurons have sex-specific functions. Synapses often form in a hybrid pattern before maturation, then sex-specific pruning retains one pattern. Cell-autonomous reversal of sexual identity in pre- or postsynaptic cells is sufficient to switch wiring. Dimorphic DMD transcription factors are necessary and sufficient; TRA-1/DMD are discussed as repressors, with extra timers needed because dmd-5/11 expression is already dimorphic early.
summaries.advanced: Neuron census figures match the companion Emmons review’s framing and the introduction here. Quantitative puncta statistics (Mann–Whitney/Kruskal–Wallis) are mentioned in figure legends without numeric medians in this extract. Catalog dataset is DS01 C. elegans (White+). PMC copy is an author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Male and hermaphrodite worms share most neurons but not all of their synapses. This paper shows many connections are wired both ways at first, then each sex prunes the extras, under the control of the cell’s sexual identity and a conserved transcription factor.
